comments.author: Don
comments.content:
Thanks for working on Quest, it's a great idea! It looks like it's got the makings to be a fantastic tool for authoring interactive fiction, especially for those with no programming experience or interest. Having tried out Inform7, I think that language is far too complex and messy for anyone setting out to write a text adventure who doesn't want to spend most of their time coding, asking for help on the forums, and fixing bugs. It's fine for people with deep programming experience (and/or lots of time on their hands), but I can never see it attracting any authors or writers outside of the small community supporting it. Writing fiction is difficult and demanding enough, and with Inform7, there's just too much writing code and problems to deal with to make it very appealing on a wider scale. However, Quest looks friendly enough for people to jump right in, or at least to take a stab at. I'll be following your development here, and I'm excited to see where you go with it.

I believe if interactive fiction is ever going to become mainstream again it's going to have to be built up from the development of easy authoring tools, something along the lines of what you're doing here with Quest. But equally important, is developing a way authors can package and sell their efforts in a commercial venue.

A game should be able to be written once, then packaged up and deployed to a variety of platforms it can be played on. This is one of Inform7's strengths, it's just unfortunate that the language is so complex that you spend much of your time writing code, instead of focusing on building a interactive story.

I don't know how the web player works, but it would be great to know if there was a way to easily build a game on Quest, then compile it into a form that could be purchased from a website, downloaded, and playable (offline) across multiple platforms (ipads, desktops, tablets, kindles, nook, ect.). That might make writing IF a more appealing venture from a commercial standpoint--the chance for an author to actually be compensated for their efforts.

Until something like that happens, it's hard to imagine interactive fiction growing much beyond a small community of IF authors writing games for each others contests.

The tools for writing IF really need to evolve and become almost transparent, and authors have to be able to make games they can sell as stand-alone products across a variety of different platforms, to make the investment of time in developing a game worthwhile.

At present writing interactive fiction seems little more than a nostalgic pastime accessible only to a small group of fans with deep programming knowledge, but it's encouraging to see tools like Quest being developed which have the potential to appeal to a wider range of writers. I hope you keep up the good work!

- Don
